title: An Old Dog Learning From an Old Trick: Lessons Learned from the September Invitation
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart reports back on a month spent tracking his own attempted Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs) -- roughly 140 brief check-ins with students in September, marked by highlighting names on a printed roster. He shares two extended stories: a disengaged student named Devony who names his class as her favorite, and a behaviorally challenging ninth grader who had written that he is "dumb," which Stuart and a colleague deliberately countered with specific evidence of his intelligence over repeated check-ins. From the month of tracking, he draws five takeaways: keeping track surfaces blind spots; the most genuine MGCs are the impromptu ones that arise while planning, grading, or doing dishes; MGCs are genuinely exhausting early in the year, especially for introverts; some students remain stubbornly hard to feel connected to; and many students actively want the one-on-one check-ins, sometimes asking for them directly. He closes by noting that even after years of using this strategy, he's still learning new things about himself, his practice, and his students through it.
points: Tracking MGCs with a physical roster surfaced Stuart's own blind spots -- quiet or "just there" students who would otherwise fall through the cracks without a systematic prompt.

The ninth-grader story shows MGCs used as a deliberate counter-narrative tool: after learning a student had written that he is "dumb," Stuart and a colleague coordinated specific, concrete evidence of his intelligence across several check-ins.

Stuart names an underdiscussed cost directly: "at the start of the year especially, MGCs are exhausting," particularly for introverts, because each check-in requires mentally "building" a full human being.

His most striking finding may be the demand side -- a student who noticed the hallway check-ins had stopped asked him directly, "When am I going to get called into the hallway?" -- evidence that more students want this than teachers might assume.
quotes: During the month of September, I attempted roughly 140 moments of genuine connection. I know this because, when I attempted an MGC, I highlighted the student's name on my printed roster.

This was significant to me because: A) She's not the kind of kid to tell you something unless it's true — she shares the brutal truth. B) It means there is at least some flicker of goodness she's experiencing in my class.
I asked, "Do you think you're smart?" "No, not really." "Okay," I said, "so here's my walkaway question to you: why do you think I think you're smart?

Keeping track is key. Keeping track of MGCs is important to me because it helps me see my blind spots. There are some students whom I'm not naturally drawn to — maybe because they are quiet or standoffish.

At the start of the year especially, MGCs are exhausting. I made a video about this. What I realized this year is that when you're first doing MGCs with your students, you're having to build human beings in your mind and heart.
A student came up to me after a few days of not doing it and said, "When am I going to get called into the hallway?" She wanted me to do this for her.
